claim: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are a family of proteins containing seven transmembrane helices.
source: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are a family of proteins containing seven transmembrane helices, with the N- and C-terminus of the protein located at the extracellular space and cytosol, respectively.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about GPCR structure.

claim: In GPCRs, the N-terminus is located at the extracellular space and the C-terminus is located in the cytosol.
source: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are a family of proteins containing seven transmembrane helices, with the N- and C-terminus of the protein located at the extracellular space and cytosol, respectively.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about GPCR topology.

claim: Ceramide or related sphingolipids might invert the topology of many GPCRs that contain a GXXXN motif in their first transmembrane helix.
source: Here, we report that ceramide or related sphingolipids might invert the topology of many GPCRs that contain a GXXXN motif in their first transmembrane helix.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis tested in the manuscript, supported by experimental data presented in the figures.

claim: In the absence of lipopolysaccharide (LPS), CCR5 adopts a topology consistent with that of GPCR, allowing mouse peritoneal macrophages to migrate toward its ligand CCL5.
source: In the absence of lipopolysaccharide (LPS), CCR5 adopts a topology consistent with that of GPCR, allowing mouse peritoneal macrophages to migrate toward its ligand CCL5.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing CCR5 detection and migration assays in the absence of LPS.

claim: LPS stimulation results in increased production of dihydroceramide.
source: LPS stimulation results in increased production of dihydroceramide, which inverts the topology of CCR5, preventing macrophages from migrating toward CCL5.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LPS-induced dihydroceramide inverts the topology of CCR5.
source: LPS stimulation results in increased production of dihydroceramide, which inverts the topology of CCR5, preventing macrophages from migrating toward CCL5.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and EM data showing changes in CCR5 topology upon LPS treatment.

claim: Topological inversion of CCR5 prevents macrophages from migrating toward CCL5.
source: LPS stimulation results in increased production of dihydroceramide, which inverts the topology of CCR5, preventing macrophages from migrating toward CCL5.
evidence: This is supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: GPCRs may not always adopt the same topology and can be regulated through topological inversion.
source: These results suggest that GPCRs may not always adopt the same topology and can be regulated through topological inversion.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: GPCRs are crucial for cell signaling.
source: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are a family of proteins containing seven transmembrane helices that are crucial for cell signaling (Rosenbaum et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rosenbaum et al., 2009.

claim: During synthesis, the N-terminal end of GPCRs is inserted into the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: A common feature of GPCRs is that their N-terminus is extracellular, which means that during synthesis their N-terminal end is inserted into lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Rosenbaum et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rosenbaum et al., 2009.

claim: The vast majority of GPCRs do not contain an N-terminal cleavable signal peptide.
source: However, the vast majority of GPCRs do not contain an N-terminal cleavable signal peptide (Guan et al., 1992), the well-characterized mechanism directing N-terminus of most secretory and transmembrane proteins into ER lumen (Zimmermann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guan et al., 1992.

claim: N-terminal cleavable signal peptide is the well-characterized mechanism directing N-terminus of most secretory and transmembrane proteins into ER lumen.
source: However, the vast majority of GPCRs do not contain an N-terminal cleavable signal peptide (Guan et al., 1992), the well-characterized mechanism directing N-terminus of most secretory and transmembrane proteins into ER lumen (Zimmermann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zimmermann et al., 2011.

claim: The difference in charge between the cytosolic and luminal loops surrounding the first transmembrane helix as well as the hydrophobicity of the first transmembrane helix of some GPCRs was reported to be crucial for translocation of their N-terminus into ER lumen.
source: The difference in charge between the cytosolic and luminal loops surrounding the first transmembrane helix as well as the hydrophobicity of the first transmembrane helix of some GPCRs was reported to be crucial for translocation of their N-terminus into ER lumen (Harley and Tipper, 1996; Wahlberg and Spiess, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harley and Tipper, 1996 and Wahlberg and Spiess, 1997.

claim: The N-terminus of TM4SF20 is inserted into ER lumen in the absence of a functional signal peptide.
source: Similar to GPCRs, the N-terminus of TM4SF20 is inserted into ER lumen in the absence of a functional signal peptide (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: A GXXXN motif in the first transmembrane helix of TM4SF20 was crucial to adopt such a topology.
source: We revealed that a GXXXN motif in the first transmembrane helix of TM4SF20 was crucial to adopt such a topology, as mutating either the glycine or asparagine residue within the motif reversed the topology of the protein by exposing the N-terminus to cytosol (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: Mutating either the glycine or asparagine residue within the GXXXN motif reversed the topology of TM4SF20 by exposing the N-terminus to cytosol.
source: We revealed that a GXXXN motif in the first transmembrane helix of TM4SF20 was crucial to adopt such a topology, as mutating either the glycine or asparagine residue within the motif reversed the topology of the protein by exposing the N-terminus to cytosol (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: The topology of TM4SF20 is inverted by ceramide or related sphingolipids as the lipid alters the direction through which the first transmembrane helix is translocated across membranes.
source: Remarkably, the topology of TM4SF20 is inverted by ceramide or related sphingolipids as the lipid alters the direction through which the first transmembrane helix is translocated across membranes (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: Regulated Alternative Translocation (RAT) does not flip transmembrane proteins that have already been synthesized but inverts the topology of newly synthesized proteins by changing the direction through which transmembrane helices are translocated across membranes.
source: Since this regulatory mechanism does not flip transmembrane proteins that have already been synthesized but inverts the topology of newly synthesized proteins by changing the direction through which transmembrane helices are translocated across membranes, we designated this process as Regulated Alternative Translocation (RAT) (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: RAT depends on the GXXXN motif, as destruction of the motif locked the protein into the inverted topology regardless of ceramide treatments.
source: This process depends on the GXXXN motif, as destruction of the motif locked the protein into the inverted topology regardless of ceramide treatments (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: Approximately 100 transmembrane proteins, most of which are GPCRs, contain a GXXXN motif in their first transmembrane helix.
source: This analysis revealed that ~100 transmembrane proteins, most of which are GPCRs, met our searching criteria (Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis performed in the study.

claim: 13 of the 16 known CC and CXC chemokine receptors contain a GXXXN motif in their first transmembrane helix.
source: Interestingly, this list contains 13 of the 16 known CC and CXC chemokine receptors (Table 1), which are GPCRs that direct migration of leukocytes and lymphocytes toward their chemokine ligands (Horuk, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis and Table 1.

claim: CC and CXC chemokine receptors are GPCRs that direct migration of leukocytes and lymphocytes toward their chemokine ligands.
source: Interestingly, this list contains 13 of the 16 known CC and CXC chemokine receptors (Table 1), which are GPCRs that direct migration of leukocytes and lymphocytes toward their chemokine ligands (Horuk, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Horuk, 2001.

claim: CCR5's physiological functions as a chemokine receptor and pathological function as a co-receptor for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) have been well characterized.
source: We selected CCR5 for characterization, as its physiological functions as a chemokine receptor and pathological function as a co-receptor for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) have been well characterized (Lederman et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lederman et al., 2006.

claim: Treatment with C6-ceramide increased the normalized fluorescent signal by approximately 70 fold in cells expressing SNAP-tag-fused CCR5.
source: Treatment with C6-ceramide, a cell permeable analogue of ceramide that is metabolically converted to natural ceramide inside cells (Denard et al., 2012), increased this normalized value by ~70 fold in cells expressing SNAP-tag-fused CCR5 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: C6-ceramide is a cell permeable analogue of ceramide that is metabolically converted to natural ceramide inside cells.
source: Treatment with C6-ceramide, a cell permeable analogue of ceramide that is metabolically converted to natural ceramide inside cells (Denard et al., 2012), increased this normalized value by ~70 fold in cells expressing SNAP-tag-fused CCR5 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Denard et al., 2012.

claim: C6-ceramide increased the normalized fluorescent signal by 10- to 150-fold in cells expressing SNAP-tag-fused CCR1, CCR4, CCR10 and MAS1.
source: C6-ceramide also increased this normalized value by 10- to 150-fold in cells expressing SNAP-tag-fused CCR1, CCR4, CCR10 and MAS1, all of which contain the GXXXN motif (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: C6-ceramide did not enhance the normalized fluorescent signal in cells expressing the SNAP-tag-fused β2-adrenergic receptor (β2AR), which does not contain the GXXXN motif.
source: In contrast, C6-ceramide did not enhance this value in cells expressing the SNAP-tag-fused β2- adrenergic receptor (β2AR), which does not contain this motif (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At least some GPCRs with the inverted topology reach the cell surface.
source: They also demonstrate that at least some of these GPCRs with the inverted topology reach the cell surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the fluorescent labeling data showing cell surface detection.

claim: The Myc-tag on C-terminally Myc-tagged CCR5 was undetectable in cells in the absence of ceramide when analyzed without saponin-mediated cell permeabilization.
source: The Myc-tag was undetectable in cells in the absence of ceramide, but was visible on cell surface in those treated with the lipid (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The Myc-tag on C-terminally Myc-tagged CCR5 was visible on cell surface in cells treated with ceramide when analyzed without saponin-mediated cell permeabilization.
source: The Myc-tag was undetectable in cells in the absence of ceramide, but was visible on cell surface in those treated with the lipid (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: CCR5 was readily detectable primarily on cell surface regardless of the ceramide treatment when cells were permeabilized by saponin.
source: As a control, we performed the same analysis in cells permeabilized by saponin. CCR5 was readily detectable primarily on cell surface regardless of the ceramide treatment under this condition (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Ceramide did not increase the immunofluorescent signal by inducing cell permeabilization.
source: In the absence of saponin, ceramide did not increase the immunofluorescent signal by inducing cell permeabilization, as treatment with the lipid under this condition did not enable detection of Giantin, a Golgi marker (Linstedt and Hauri, 1993) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by control experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Giantin is a Golgi marker.
source: In the absence of saponin, ceramide did not increase the immunofluorescent signal by inducing cell permeabilization, as treatment with the lipid under this condition did not enable detection of Giantin, a Golgi marker (Linstedt and Hauri, 1993) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Linstedt and Hauri, 1993.

claim: The N-terminal domain of CCR5(A) contains four O-linked glycosylation sites (S6, S7, T16, S17), which are the only sites where CCR5 is glycosylated.
source: In CCR5 produced under normal circumstance (CCR5(A)), this extracellular region (Duma et al., 2007) contains four O-linked glycosylation sites (S6, S7, T16, S17), which are the only sites where CCR5 is glycosylated (Bannert et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Duma et al., 2007 and Bannert et al., 2001.

claim: The apparent molecular weight of CCR5(B) is expected to be lower than that of CCR5(A), because CCR5(B) should not be glycosylated.
source: Since the extracellular regions of CCR5(B) do not contain any consensus sites for glycosylation, the apparent molecular weight of CCR5(B) is expected to be lower than that of CCR5(A), because CCR5(B) should not be glycosylated (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the predicted topology and glycosylation sites.

claim: Treatment with C6-ceramide gradually increased the amount of another form of CCR5 with a lower molecular weight.
source: Immunoblot analysis revealed that in the absence of ceramide, CCR5 migrated at the established molecular weight (Figure 2B, lane 1). Treatment with C6-ceramide gradually increased the amount of another form of the protein with a lower molecular weight (Figure 2B, lanes 2–6).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mutating all four glycosylation sites to alanine (S6A, S7A, T16A, and S17A) did not block ceramide-induced RAT of CCR5.
source: These mutations did not block ceramide-induced RAT of CCR5 judging by the localization of C-terminus of the protein using the assay shown in Figure 1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The apparent molecular weight of the B form of the mutant CCR5 (S6A, S7A, T16A, S17A) produced in ceramide-treated cells was the same as that of the A form produced in untreated cells.
source: The apparent molecular weight of the B form of the mutant CCR5 produced in ceramide-treated cells was the same as that of the A form produced in untreated cells (Figure 2C, lanes 3 and 4), and it was identical to that of wildtype CCR5(B), which was also unglycosylated (Figure 2C, lanes 2–4).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: N-terminally SNAP-tagged CCR5 is active in ligand binding.
source: We also used N-terminally SNAP-tagged CCR5 known to be active in ligand binding (Orlandi et al., 2016) to determine the localization of the N-terminus of the protein.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Orlandi et al., 2016.

claim: Fluorescent labeling by a cell-impermeable reagent was detected in cells expressing N-terminally SNAP-tagged CCR5 incubated in the absence of C6-ceramide but not those in the presence of the lipid.
source: Consistent with the model shown in Figure 2A, fluorescent labeling by a cell-impermeable reagent was detected in cells incubated in the absence of C6-ceramide but not those in the presence of the lipid (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescent labeling data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: C6-ceramide treatment did not affect expression of N-terminally SNAP-tagged CCR5.
source: Immunoblot analysis indicated that C6-ceramide treatment did not affect expression of the fusion protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Addition of an N-terminal signal peptide does not affect ceramide-induced RAT of TM4SF20.
source: It should be pointed out that the N-terminally SNAP-tagged CCR5 used in these experiments contains a signal peptide derived from CD8 at the N-terminus. Our previous study demonstrates that addition of an N-terminal signal peptide does not affect ceramide-induced RAT of TM4SF20, a transmembrane protein containing the GXXXN motif in the first transmembrane helix (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: The CCR5 topology reporter protein expressed in cells cultured in the absence of ceramide was biotinylated by a cell surface sulfhydryl reactive biotinylation reagent and precipitable by streptavidin beads.
source: The reporter protein was precipitated by streptavidin-conjugated beads in the absence of C6-ceramide, an observation indicating that the mutations made in the reporter protein did not affect transport of the protein to cell surface (Figure 2F, lanes 3 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by biotin labeling and precipitation data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The CCR5 topology reporter protein was not precipitated by streptavidin beads in cells treated with C6-ceramide.
source: In contrast, the reporter protein was not precipitated at all in cells treated with C6-ceramide (Figure 2F, lanes 4 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by biotin labeling and precipitation data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Wildtype CCR5 was precipitated by streptavidin beads regardless of ceramide treatment.
source: As a control, we also performed the same experiment with wildtype CCR5, which contains cysteine residues on both sides of membranes (Figure 2G). Wildtype CCR5 was precipitated by streptavidin beads regardless of ceramide treatment (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by biotin labeling and precipitation data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: CCR5(B) produced in the presence of ceramide was on the cell surface.
source: These observations demonstrated that CCR5(B) produced in the presence of ceramide was also on the cell surface, ruling out the possibility that the result shown in Figure 2F was caused by ceramide-induced internalization of CCR5.
evidence: This is inferred from the biotin labeling experiments comparing wildtype and reporter CCR5.

claim: LPS was reported to stimulate production of ceramide in mouse macrophage-like RAW264.7 cells.
source: LPS was reported to stimulate production of ceramide in mouse macrophage-like RAW264.7 cells (Sims et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sims et al., 2010.

claim: Treatment of mouse peritoneal macrophages with LPS increased production of dihydroceramide but not ceramide.
source: Unlike RAW264.7 cells, we observed that treatment of mouse peritoneal macrophages with LPS increased production of dihydroceramide but not ceramide (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Dihydroceramide is structurally similar to ceramide and has been shown to perform functions previously attributed to ceramide.
source: Since dihydroceramide is structurally similar to ceramide and has been shown to perform functions previously attributed to ceramide (Siddique et al., 2015), we hypothesized that LPS-induced production of dihydroceramide may also induce RAT of CCR5.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Siddique et al., 2015.

claim: CCR5 was detected through immunofluorescent microscopy without cell permeabilization in macrophages cultured in the absence but not in the presence of LPS.
source: CCR5 was detected through this method in macrophages cultured in the absence but not in the presence of LPS (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: CCR5 was readily detectable on cell surface of macrophages regardless of the LPS treatment when cells were permeabilized.
source: As a control, we also performed the same analysis in permeabilized macrophages. CCR5 was readily detectable on cell surface regardless of the LPS treatment under this condition (Figure 3D and E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for images with properly adjusted intensity).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Treatment with fumonisin B1 (FB1) prevented LPS from inducing production of dihydroceramide.
source: To confirm that LPS stimulates RAT of CCR5 through increased production of dihydroceramide, we treated macrophages with fumonisin B1 (FB1), an inhibitor of ceramide synthase that catalyzes formation of the sphingolipid (Kitatani et al., 2008). Treatment with FB1 prevented LPS from inducing production of dihydroceramide (Figure 3A), and rendered the N-terminus of CCR5 to be detected by fluorescent microscopy regardless of treatment with LPS and cell permeabilization (Figure 3F–I).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: FB1 is an inhibitor of ceramide synthase that catalyzes formation of the sphingolipid.
source: To confirm that LPS stimulates RAT of CCR5 through increased production of dihydroceramide, we treated macrophages with fumonisin B1 (FB1), an inhibitor of ceramide synthase that catalyzes formation of the sphingolipid (Kitatani et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kitatani et al., 2008.

claim: Treatment with FB1 rendered the N-terminus of CCR5 to be detected by fluorescent microscopy regardless of treatment with LPS and cell permeabilization.
source: Treatment with FB1 prevented LPS from inducing production of dihydroceramide (Figure 3A), and rendered the N-terminus of CCR5 to be detected by fluorescent microscopy regardless of treatment with LPS and cell permeabilization (Figure 3F–I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3F–I.

claim: In the absence of LPS, gold particle clusters labeling CCR5 were found on extracellular side of plasma membranes.
source: In the absence of LPS, the gold particle clusterswere found on extracellular side of plasma membranes (Figure 3J, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immuno-gold EM data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: In cells treated with LPS, gold particle clusters labeling CCR5 were found on intracellular side of plasma membranes but not endocytic vesicles.
source: These particles were found on intracellular side of plasma membranes but not endocytic vesicles in cells treated with LPS (Figure 3K, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immuno-gold EM data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: The vast majority of CCR5 labeled by gold clusters had its N-terminus at the extracellular and intracellular side of plasma membranes, respectively, in cells cultured in the absence and presence of LPS.
source: After counting ~20 macrophages cultured in either condition, we found that the vast majority of CCR5 labeled by gold clusters had its N-terminus at the extracellular and intracellular side of plasma membranes, respectively, in cells cultured in the absence and presence of LPS (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immuno-gold EM data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: LPS induced RAT of CCR5 in macrophages isolated from mice injected intraperitoneally with LPS.
source: Under this condition, LPS also induced RAT of CCR5 in macrophages, and this topological inversion was inhibited by co-injection of FB1 (Figure 4A–L).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Co-injection of FB1 inhibited LPS-induced topological inversion of CCR5 in macrophages isolated from mice injected intraperitoneally with LPS.
source: Under this condition, LPS also induced RAT of CCR5 in macrophages, and this topological inversion was inhibited by co-injection of FB1 (Figure 4A–L).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The N-terminal domain of CCR5 is in direct contact with chemokine ligands.
source: Since the N-terminal domain of CCR5 is in direct contact with chemokine ligands (Duma et al., 2007), LPS-induced topological inversion, which places this region into cytosol, should block the receptor from binding to the extracellular chemokine ligands thereby preventing macrophages from migrating toward these chemokine ligands.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duma et al., 2007.

claim: Treatment with LPS completely blocked migration of macrophages toward CCL5.
source: As expected, treatment with LPS completely blocked migration of macrophages toward CCL5 (Figure 5A), a known ligand for CCR5 (Samson et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CCL5 is a known ligand for CCR5.
source: As expected, treatment with LPS completely blocked migration of macrophages toward CCL5 (Figure 5A), a known ligand for CCR5 (Samson et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Samson et al., 1997.

claim: Migration of macrophages toward CCL5 in the absence of LPS was strictly dependent on CCR5.
source: The migration observed in the absence of LPS was strictly dependent on CCR5, as such migration was not detected in Ccr5-/- macrophages (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by migration assay data comparing wildtype and Ccr5-/- macrophages shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Co-treatment with FB1 eliminated the inhibitory effect of LPS on migration of macrophages toward CCL5.
source: If LPS blocks migration of macrophages toward CCL5 by stimulating RAT of CCR5, then FB1, which prevents LPS from inducing RAT of CCR5 by inhibiting production of dihydroceramide (Figure 3F–I), should relieve this blockade. Indeed, co-treatment with FB1 eliminated the inhibitory effect of LPS on migration of macrophages toward CCL5 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Upon bacterial infection, cells surrounding the infected tissue secrete chemokines including CCL5.
source: Upon bacterial infection, cells surrounding the infected tissue secrete chemokines including CCL5 (Horuk, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Horuk, 2001.

claim: In unprimed macrophages, CCL5 interacts with the GPCR configuration of CCR5 (CCR5(A)), attracting migration of these cells toward the infected sites.
source: In unprimed macrophages, CCL5 interacts with the GPCR configuration of CCR5 (CCR5(A)), attracting migration of these cells toward the infected sites.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Upon encounter with bacterial byproducts such as LPS, the increased production of dihydroceramide in macrophages triggers RAT of CCR5.
source: Upon encounter with bacterial byproducts such as LPS, the increased production of dihydroceramide in macrophages triggers RAT of CCR5, resulting in production of the protein with an inverted topology (CCR5(B)).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing LPS-induced dihydroceramide production and CCR5 topology inversion.

claim: Topological inversion of CCR5 blocks macrophages from further migration toward CCL5.
source: This topological inversion blocks macrophages from further migration toward CCL5, allowing macrophages to produce pro-inflammatory cytokines to combat infection at the current location instead of migrating to the cells from which CCL5 is secreted, as these cells themselves may not be infected.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the experimental findings.

claim: RAT of CCR5 and other CC and CXC families of chemokine receptors containing a GXXXN motif in their first transmembrane helix may explain why macrophages overwhelmed by LPS during sepsis are markedly less effective in clearing bacterial infection.
source: On the other hand, RAT of CCR5 and other CC and CXC families of chemokine receptors containing a GXXXN motif in their first transmembrane helix may explain why macrophages overwhelmed by LPS during sepsis are markedly less effective in clearing bacterial infection, as they may be less sensitive to chemotaxis reaction (Biswas and Lopez-Collazo, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting the findings to sepsis, supported by citation to Biswas and Lopez-Collazo, 2009.

claim: Macrophages overwhelmed by LPS during sepsis are markedly less effective in clearing bacterial infection.
source: On the other hand, RAT of CCR5 and other CC and CXC families of chemokine receptors containing a GXXXN motif in their first transmembrane helix may explain why macrophages overwhelmed by LPS during sepsis are markedly less effective in clearing bacterial infection, as they may be less sensitive to chemotaxis reaction (Biswas and Lopez-Collazo, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Biswas and Lopez-Collazo, 2009.

claim: CXCR4 is a chemokine receptor that has been identified as a co-receptor for HIV.
source: In addition to CCR5, CXCR4, another chemokine receptor that has been identified as a co-receptor for HIV (Lederman et al., 2006), also contains the GXXXN motif in the first transmembrane helix, and therefore is likely subjected to topological regulation through RAT as well.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lederman et al., 2006.

claim: CXCR4 contains the GXXXN motif in the first transmembrane helix.
source: In addition to CCR5, CXCR4, another chemokine receptor that has been identified as a co-receptor for HIV (Lederman et al., 2006), also contains the GXXXN motif in the first transmembrane helix, and therefore is likely subjected to topological regulation through RAT as well.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis and Table 1.

claim: CXCR4 is likely subjected to topological regulation through RAT.
source: In addition to CCR5, CXCR4, another chemokine receptor that has been identified as a co-receptor for HIV (Lederman et al., 2006), also contains the GXXXN motif in the first transmembrane helix, and therefore is likely subjected to topological regulation through RAT as well.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of the GXXXN motif and the findings with CCR5.

claim: HIV directly interacts with the N-terminal domain and the second extracellular loop of CCR5 and CXCR4 with a topology consistent with that of GPCRs.
source: Since HIV directly interacts with the N-terminal domain and the second extracellular loop of CCR5 and CXCR4 with a topology consistent with that of GPCRs (Dogo-Isonagie et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2007; Lu et al., 1997), topological inversion of these receptors through RAT should block HIV entry as the regions binding the virus should be located intracellularly thereby inaccessible to the virus in circulation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dogo-Isonagie et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2007; Lu et al., 1997.

claim: Topological inversion of CCR5 and CXCR4 through RAT should block HIV entry.
source: Since HIV directly interacts with the N-terminal domain and the second extracellular loop of CCR5 and CXCR4 with a topology consistent with that of GPCRs (Dogo-Isonagie et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2007; Lu et al., 1997), topological inversion of these receptors through RAT should block HIV entry as the regions binding the virus should be located intracellularly thereby inaccessible to the virus in circulation.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mechanism of HIV entry and the predicted topology inversion.

claim: LPS or other treatments increasing intracellular levels of ceramide led to resistance in HIV infection.
source: This notion is consistent with previous reports showing that LPS or other treatments increasing intracellular levels of ceramide led to resistance in HIV infection (Bernstein et al., 1991; Finnegan et al., 2004; Kornbluth et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bernstein et al., 1991; Finnegan et al., 2004; Kornbluth et al., 1989.

claim: Compounds capable of inducing RAT of CCR5 and CXCR4 but without toxicity associated with LPS may be particularly effective in combating HIV infection.
source: These observations suggest that compounds capable of inducing RAT of these chemokine receptors but without toxicity associated with LPS may be particularly effective in combating HIV infection, as the single treatment may block both receptors from supporting entry of HIV.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on the findings.

claim: FB1 blocked LPS-induced topological inversion of CCR5 by inhibiting synthesis of dihydroceramide.
source: This conclusion is supported by our observations that FB1, which blocked LPS-induced topological inversion of CCR5 by inhibiting synthesis of dihydroceramide, restored the chemotaxis reaction of macrophages exposed to LPS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing FB1 effects on dihydroceramide production and CCR5 topology.

claim: FB1 restored the chemotaxis reaction of macrophages exposed to LPS.
source: This conclusion is supported by our observations that FB1, which blocked LPS-induced topological inversion of CCR5 by inhibiting synthesis of dihydroceramide, restored the chemotaxis reaction of macrophages exposed to LPS.
evidence: This is supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Most CC and CXC families of chemokine receptors contain a GXXXN motif in their first transmembrane helix.
source: Since most CC and CXC families of chemokine receptors contain a GXXXN motif in their first transmembrane helix, LPS may invert the topology of all these chemokine receptors.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis and Table 1.

claim: LPS may invert the topology of all CC and CXC chemokine receptors that contain a GXXXN motif.
source: Since most CC and CXC families of chemokine receptors contain a GXXXN motif in their first transmembrane helix, LPS may invert the topology of all these chemokine receptors.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from the CCR5 findings.

claim: Mice deficient in ceramide synthase 6 over-recruited macrophages to the inflammatory sites because of enhanced chemotaxis.
source: This scenario may explain why mice deficient in ceramide synthase 6, the major ceramide synthase expressed in macrophages, over-recruited macrophages to the inflammatory sites because of enhanced chemotaxis (Eberle et al., 2015), as the lack of production of dihydroceramide may not be able to inhibit these chemokine receptors through topological inversion.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eberle et al., 2015.

claim: Ceramide synthase 6 is the major ceramide synthase expressed in macrophages.
source: This scenario may explain why mice deficient in ceramide synthase 6, the major ceramide synthase expressed in macrophages, over-recruited macrophages to the inflammatory sites because of enhanced chemotaxis (Eberle et al., 2015), as the lack of production of dihydroceramide may not be able to inhibit these chemokine receptors through topological inversion.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eberle et al., 2015.

claim: CCR5 can be desensitized through arrestin-mediated internalization.
source: However, since CCR5 can be desensitized through other mechanism such as arrestin-mediated internalization (Oppermann, 2004), it remains unclear whether topological inversion through RAT is the only mechanism through which LPS inhibits CCR5 activity as a chemokine receptor.

claim: It remains unclear whether topological inversion through RAT is the only mechanism through which LPS inhibits CCR5 activity as a chemokine receptor.

source: Likewise, the N-terminally SNAP-tagged CCR5 construct used in the current study contains a signal peptide from human CD8, but the protein still underwent ceramide-induced RAT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing topology inversion of N-terminally SNAP-tagged CCR5.

claim: Ceramide treatment blocked O-linked glycosylation of CCR5.
source: This model may also be consistent with the observation that ceramide treatment blocked O-linked glycosylation of CCR5, as this post-translational modification takes place in the Golgi complex.

claim: O-linked glycosylation takes place in the Golgi complex.
source: This model may also be consistent with the observation that ceramide treatment blocked O-linked glycosylation of CCR5, as this post-translational modification takes place in the Golgi complex.

source: This model is also inconsistent with the observation that significant amount of CCR5 in cells treated with ceramide or macrophages treated with LPS, which stimulated production of dihydroceramide, was localized on cell surface.

claim: Membrane proteins can be regulated by topological inversion through RAT.
source: A major implication of the current study is that membrane proteins can be regulated by topological inversion through RAT.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Ceramide stimulates RAT of TM4SF20, and this reaction depends on the presence of a GXXXN motif in the first transmembrane helix of the protein.
source: We have previously reported that ceramide stimulates RAT of TM4SF20, and this reaction depends on the presence of a GXXXN motif in the first transmembrane helix of the protein (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: Most proteins containing a GXXXN motif in their first transmembrane helix are GPCRs.
source: In the present study we identified ~100 proteins containing this motif in their first transmembrane helix, and demonstrated that CCR5, one of the proteins in the list, can indeed be regulated through RAT. Interestingly, most proteins in the list including CCR5 are GPCRs.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis.

claim: In order for GPCRs to function as GPCRs, the N-terminal end of the first transmembrane helix has to insert into ER lumen.
source: In order for these proteins to function as GPCRs, the N-terminal end of the first transmembrane helix has to insert into ER lumen (Pierce et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pierce et al., 2002.

claim: The presence of a GXXXN motif within the first transmembrane helix of many GPCRs may be a previously unrecognized mechanism for the transmembrane helix to be inserted with the N-terminus in the ER lumen.
source: Our finding suggests that the presence of a GXXXN motif within the first transmembrane helix of many GPCRs may be a previously unrecognized mechanism for the transmembrane helix to be inserted with such an orientation.
evidence: This is a novel interpretation of the findings.

claim: The presence of the GXXXN motif may allow GPCRs to be regulated through topological inversion upon accumulation of dihydroceramide, ceramide or other related sphingolipids.

evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from the findings.

claim: Topological inversion of GPCRs not only inhibits functions of the GPCR, but also simultaneously activates functions performed by the protein with the inversed topology.
source: Such regulation not only inhibits functions of the GPCR, but also simultaneously activates functions performed by the protein with the inversed topology.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the potential consequences of topology inversion.

claim: Proteins sharing the architecture of GPCRs that contain seven transmembrane helices but adopting an inverted topology have been reported to function as receptors independent of G proteins.
source: Proteins sharing the architecture of GPCRs that contain seven transmembrane helices but adopting an inverted topology have been reported to function as receptors independent of G proteins (Deckert et al., 2006) and ion channels (Sato et al., 2008).

claim: When the N48L mutation was made in CCR5, the mutant protein was exclusively localized in the ER.
source: However, when we made a similar mutation in CCR5 (CCR5(N48L)), we observed that unlike wild type CCR5 with the inverted topology (CCR5(B)) that is capable of reaching cell surface, the mutant protein was exclusively localized in the ER.
evidence: This is an observation from experiments attempting to lock CCR5 topology.
